title: Lee Collins at the Astoria and the Damp Weather recording
summary: Sayles recalls the Astoria band under Lee Collins and David Jones and the Victor recording at Italian Hall: the rehearsed numbers, tunes made up in the studio and Joe Strada replacing Albert Martin.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: You missed out the, uh, the Lee Collins period there. Well, I, well, that, oh, yeah, that's right,

that's right. That was, that was before Sidney Desmond, I mean Sidney Desmond, because there was, there was a fella named John Morell, banjo player. He had a job at the La Vida, as a jitney dance. That's right. And, um, and that band was, the leader was John Morell, the banjo player, and, uh, Lee Collins on trumpet. Thereto Poinnell on alto and David Jones on tenor. Yeah. Uh, Joe Rovershaw on piano, uh, and, uh, Albert Martin, I think, the drummer. Oh, Albert Martin. Yeah. On drum, and I took John Morell's play. Well, at that time, the Lyric Theater was, it was, uh, was closed in that year, and they had a show here, and they were just training around here, so Binge got the idea of taking the show and, and building this band with, uh, with Lee Collins and David Jones as the leader of it, see. I think that's why we made that, uh, that record while we were making, working there, because we used to play those numbers every night, I remember. Tell me about that, uh, recording date. How did you come by that? Well, that was, Lee Collins, that was true, Lee Collins. This fellow, uh, was named the same fellow on the Southland, I believe? Was that, that was the same, Mares? Yeah, Mares. Yeah, well, he liked it, Lee and everything, and some fellas had told him that they, they should record Lee, so, I think the company came from, from New York. It was Victor Company. Yeah, Victor, that's right, it was, on, on the Bluebird, Bluebird record, yeah. Well, we, we, we, we made that recording down at, uh, the Italian Hall on Espanola. Yeah. Uh-huh. What time of day was that when you started? Can you remember? Oh, we started that when we got there in the morning around about nine or ten o'clock, I'll never forget. Yeah, I think we stayed there until about six or seven o'clock that evening. Yeah? Mm-hmm. It was a pretty, uh, wet day, wasn't it? Yeah, it was raining, and, uh, and, uh, I wouldn't say it was so cold, but, I mean, the window was long, New Orleans rain, you see? Is that where you got the name of that tune from? Yeah, Damp Weather. Well, our first tune we had, I remember we got together was Astor, Strut, and, uh, uh, now, maybe you can tell me, uh, those are the tunes we were hoisting on. Tip Easy Blues. No, that, we made that up in the station, at the, at the, well, at the, during the recording, and also Damp Weather. And, uh, Duet Stump? Yeah, Duet Stump. Those two were the real numbers that we had really gotten down really good together, see? Yeah. So, the other time, we just made them up, like you said, the one blues, and one guy said, well, go ahead, rain, I'll just name it,
this damp weather, see? Everybody was kind of white. And there wasn't one named Tip Easy or something? Tip Easy. Yeah, like, well, we had all,

Because he came through town to Texas, and he had, um, he took members, they took fellows out of three or four bands around here, you see? And, uh, that's where I, I didn't go, so, uh, that's why they picked up Joe Strada. Joe Strada. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Picked him up, that's why he was actually on the session. Yeah. So it wasn't Albert Martin on the session? No,
